items.title: You've stood with me. Here's what's next.
items.author: 1axbkddtc87p0ndwzoslnw6i979x1i1ymvs1ib@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Election Day is 30 days away, and the fight for free and fair elections is here. In some states, early voting has already begun, and nearly every state has sent out mail-in ballots.

I have been on the road the last week traveling. I apologize that some of my essays have been shorter and videos less well-produced.

For months, we have been building toward this moment. Campaigns are communicating with voters and executing get-out-the-vote plans. Nonprofit groups are registering voters and recruiting poll workers.

Then there are the lawyers. My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in more than 40 states. We have beaten the Department of Justice more than 20 times, defended voting by mail against Trump's executive orders, and won three times at the Supreme Court to keep Missouri from using an illegally gerrymandered map.

But that is only part of the fight.

Democracy Docket is tracking almost 200 cases in nearly all 50 states and D.C. Keeping a spotlight on what is happening to democracy in the courts is a critical part of the effort to protect our elections.

Since Trump returned to office, Democracy Docket has closely tracked his authoritarian schemes. While other media outlets have bent the knee, Democracy Docket has remained unbowed.

I created Democracy Docket for moments like this. And you, our readers, have been with me the entire time.

When I'm tired, your words energize me. Your support helps me fight another day. I will never forget that.

No matter what happens on Election Day, and no matter what Trump does or threatens, I promise you this: Democracy Docket will keep fighting.

As a subscriber, you know that everything on the Democracy Docket website and in its flagship newsletters is available to everyone. All its reporting and video content is free.

What you may not know is that Democracy Docket also offers a premium membership for people who want deeper analysis. Premium members receive my exclusive analysis and are invited to member-only briefings and events.

Most importantly, premium members sustain Democracy Docket's independent, pro-democracy mission. It has no corporate parent or investors. There are no venture capitalists or private equity backers. It does not rely on ActBlue or Substack.

To put it simply, it relies on you.

With Election Day right around the corner, we will have to work harder than ever. If you haven't upgraded to a premium membership, please consider doing so today. Become part of the community that powers Democracy Docket's work and protects our democracy.

If now isn't the right moment for you, I understand, and I thank you for being a loyal reader. Every one of you is an important part of our team and of this mission.

We are all in this fight together, and I couldn't do it without you. We have an important fight ahead in just 30 days, but I know we will win — together.

items.title: America’s latest electoral fault line: Israel
items.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708488-d186966748@mail194.suw241.rsgsv.net
items.content:
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took the stage at the United Nations last month, diplomats streamed for the exits. Three years after October 7, when much of the Western world rallied behind Israel in the wake of Hamas’ attack, the political ground has shifted.

Some of the biggest changes are happening here in the US. Two years ago, Abbas Alawieh helped lead the Uncommitted movement, pressuring Democrats over Gaza. Now he’s running for Michigan state Senate, and Kamala Harris is calling him. Elsewhere in Michigan, AIPAC and its allies spent close to $30 million backing Abdul El-Sayed’s opponent in the Democratic Senate primary. El-Sayed won anyway.

For some voters, the prominence of Israel itself is striking.

“I don’t know why Israel has become the pivotal point,” said Mimi Price-Miletic, a Democratic voter in Michigan. “There are so many issues in this country that we should be dealing with, and you’re worried about what’s happening, like, millions of miles away?”

And the divide crosses party lines. Younger Republicans are questioning US support for Israel, even as party leaders advance deeper defense cooperation. 

Meanwhile, AIPAC faces new challenges to its influence, as younger Jewish political groups, like J Street and Jewish Voice for Peace, offer sharply different visions for what should come next.

, reporter Najib Aminy follows the new fault lines forming around the US–Israel relationship and asks: As the old political consensus is tested, who gets to shape what replaces it?

items.title: Will your mail ballot be affected by new Postal Service changes?
items.author: 1axb0o42qvoqvr8bgo10g53n43qas3mp5pnav3@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Hello, pro-democracy readers! Happy Friday. The Postal Service is slowing its pickup and delivery times for much of the country. As part of our detailed report on how these changes could impact voters, the Democracy Docket team built a map to help you figure out whether your ballot will be affected.

Meanwhile, a new poll found that a majority of Americans overwhelmingly support pro-voting policies like early in-person voting options. Ironically, 75% of those polled supported giving more resources to the Postal Service.

P.S. — Don’t forget to scroll down to the bottom of today’s newsletter to check out this week’s good news.

All that and more is on the docket today. See you next week!

items.title: Why top Texas election denier Ken Paxton could cause chaos if he loses his Senate race
items.author: 1axb4tfa76e59b2esfskm9005uz0lpny82asbn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
It’s October, Halloween is coming, and I can’t think of anything more frightening than the enormous federal resources that Trump has directed to try to prove that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him. (OK, maybe “The Blair Witch Project” or “The Exorcist” are scarier — but at least those are only movies).

Luckily, the horror show that is the Trump administration’s effort to find mass voter fraud and relitigate the 2020 election has fallen flat. With all the chaos and noise Trump and his allies are creating around the midterms, it’s easy to forget that the election deniers are losing.

But this week was a good reminder: Not one, but two Trump administration officials tasked at least in part with proving 2020 voter conspiracies abruptly resigned — and both quit without proving anything. First was Kurt Olsen, a hardcore Trump loyalist who led a special White House task force probing 2020 election conspiracies, then moved to the Department of Justice.

The other was Andrew Bailey, a former Missouri attorney general and avowed election denier, who was the FBI's co-deputy director and helped lead the bureau’s raid on a Fulton County, Georgia election hub earlier this year.

They’re the latest in a string of resignations of administration appointees who were brought in to prove 2020 election conspiracy theories, or indict the president’s political enemies, and utterly failed to do so. Nearly half a dozen election deniers recently resigned — and there’s still no evidence that the 2020 election was rigged.
